documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in military systems to support intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance, autonomous operations, logistics, command and control, and decision support. Effective use, however, depends not only on technical performance but also on how operators perceive, interpret, evaluate, and rely on AI outputs under uncertainty, time pressure, and adversarial interference. This study presents a conceptual integrative review informed by a structured supplementary literature search and synthesis. It synthesizes human factors, human–automation trust, human–AI teaming, military AI, and industrial engineering literature to develop an iterative multistage framework of human–AI trust in military applications. Trust is conceptualized as dynamic situational trust in a specific military AI system during task interaction, while dispositional, initial, and learned trust are treated as antecedent conditions. The framework distinguishes four analytically separable but functionally interdependent stages—perception, interpretation, evaluation, and trust judgment and reliance decision—and identifies four military-relevant moderators: system transparency, explainability, and behavioral predictability; data quality and information uncertainty; adversarial vulnerability; and operational and organizational context. The framework clarifies conceptual pathways to calibrated reliance, overtrust, and undertrust, and derives implications for task analysis, interface evaluation, human-centered design, operator training, and empirical validation.

Purpose This study aims to analyze the linear structural relationships and nonlinear predictive contributions associated with tourist satisfaction in the Trusmi Batik Tourism Area. By integrating PLS-SEM, ANN, and SHAP-based XAI, it evaluates how destination attributes function as hygiene or motivator factors. The ultimate goal is to develop a strategic quadrant matrix to guide local governments and destination managers in optimizing craft-based cultural tourism management. Design/methodology/approach This study employs a multi-stage hybrid design integrating PLS-SEM, an MLP-based artificial neural network (ANN) and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) using SHAP analysis. PLS-SEM evaluates linear structural relationships based on the proposed theoretical hypotheses. A parsimonious single-hidden-layer ANN captures complex, nonlinear predictive patterns. Finally, SHAP values interpret the model's hidden predictive contributions to construct an actionable strategic quadrant matrix. Findings The findings suggest that accessibility, resources, and the environment emerged as the primary “Star” motivators, with accessibility showing the strongest structural contribution and predictive importance among the examined constructs (ß = 0.310; |ϕ| = 0.416). “Batik Arts” emerged as the most influential indicator within the dataset. Services occupied the “Foundation” quadrant, whereas Facilities functioned primarily as a baseline hygiene factor and did not exhibit a statistically significant structural relationship with tourist satisfaction (ß = 0.014, p = 0.888). The parsimonious single-hidden-layer ANN demonstrated promising predictive performance in capturing nonlinear patterns within this exploratory dataset. Research limitations/implications This study integrates PLS-SEM, ANN, and SHAP-based XAI to examine linear and nonlinear patterns associated with tourist satisfaction within craft-based cultural tourism destinations. The findings suggest prioritizing immersive batik workshops, walkable heritage corridors, digital visitor information, and routine maintenance of basic facilities. The small, geographically focused sample limits generalizability and supports the need for external validation using larger and more diverse datasets. Practical implications This study offers a practical reference for tourism operators and local authorities to improve strategic resource allocation. Instead of funding costly luxury hotel expansions, managers could prioritize maintaining hygiene assets, including toilets, seating, and worship facilities. To enhance visitor satisfaction, investments may emphasize “Star” motivators through immersive batik-making workshops and authentic cultural experiences. Local governments may also improve urban micro-mobility by developing walkable sidewalks and flexible motorcycle routes throughout Trusmi's historic heritage corridors. These evidence-based recommendations support sustainable destination management while strengthening visitor experiences, cultural preservation, and long-term tourism resilience. Social implications This study has social implications for sustaining craft-based cultural tourism while strengthening community participation and cultural identity. The findings highlight the importance of accessible public spaces, immersive batik-making experiences, reliable visitor services, and heritage storytelling in supporting visitor engagement. Prioritizing these attributes can help local governments and tourism operators create more inclusive tourism environments that benefit visitors, artisans, and local communities. The framework also supports balanced resource allocation between basic hygiene facilities and culturally distinctive motivators. By strengthening artisan involvement, digital cultural communication, and heritage preservation, the approach can contribute to community resilience, intergenerational knowledge transmission, and sustainable tourism development. Originality/value The value of this study lies in its innovative hybrid framework integrating PLS-SEM, MLP-based ANN, and Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) within cultural tourism research. Compared with conventional linear approaches, the framework combines structural relationships, nonlinear predictive patterns, and SHAP-based interpretability to identify destination attributes with different levels of strategic importance.

The objective of the study is to investigate unethical issues in the use of Artificial intelligence (AI) among undergraduates in public Universities in Cross River State. The study was conducted in University of Calabar and University of Cross River State. Survey research design was adopted of the study. The population of this study comprised all final year students in the two public Universities in Cross River State. The population of final year students in University of Calabar and University of Cross River State comprised of 7,020 undergraduate students as recorded by Academic Planning Unit & Management Information System, 2023/2024 of the respective Universities. Stratified random sampling was adopted for the study. A total sample of 409 students which constitute 10% of the population of students in the study area sampling from population of 4081 students from fifty three (53) departments of University of Calabar and University of Cross River State. A questionnaire titled Unethical issues in the Use of Artificial intelligence Questionnaire (UIUAIQ) was developed by the researchers. This was subjected to face and content validity by three experts in measurement and evaluation in Faculty of Education University of Calabar. A trial tested on fifty (50) students from College of Health Technology Calabar to establish the reliability of the instrument. Cronbach Alpha coefficient was used to determine the reliability estimate of the instrument α = .70-.72. The instrument was administered to the respondents and retrieved with Zero attrition rate. This process was facilitated by the researcher and two trained research assistants. The data collected was analyzed through descriptive statistics of mean and standard deviation. The findings of this study reveal a significant prevalence of unethical issues in the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) among undergraduates in public universities in Cross River State. Furthermore, the study also indicates a high level of overreliance on AI technologies among undergraduates, leading to reduced engagement in academic tasks and a decline in deep learning experiences. Based on the findings, it was recommended among others that Higher institutions should incorporate AI ethics education into their curriculum to sensitize students about the ethical implications of AI misuse.

documents.abstract: Generative AI has entered software work with remarkable speed, yet trust in its output remains unsettled. This study examines how developers and learners navigate AI-assisted software work through mental models and trust. Analyzing 40,052 responses from the 2025 Stack Overflow Developer Survey, the findings reveal a durable paradox: professionals use AI more intensively than learners but trust it less, evaluating its capability for complex tasks more cautiously. The primary threat to trust is corrective labor, such as debugging time, rather than code legibility. Cluster analysis identifies four mental-model profiles—open but light users, skeptical dependents, resistant/disengaged respondents, and enthusiastic adopters—with professionals disproportionately concentrated in skeptical dependence. Ultimately, adoption does not settle the trust question; instead, mental models act as interpretive filters through which developers decide when to rely, verify, and pull back.

IntroductionEffective patient communication is an essential skill for radiology and nuclear medicine specialists, yet it remains underemphasized in residency training. With increasing patient access to electronic medical records, the ability to translate technical reports into patient-facing summaries is critical. Generative AI may offer a dual benefit of improving workflow by producing patient-appropriate summaries and serving as a training tool to help residents hone their communication skills. MethodsSeventy-six de-identified nuclear medicine imaging procedure reports (covering general nuclear medicine, PET/CT (positron emission tomography-computed tomography), and nuclear cardiology) were used to generate 608 patient-facing summaries: four versions of each report were generated using ChatGPT models (o1-mini, 4o, 4o-mini, 4 legacy) and four versions were written by residents. Summaries adhered to a four-sentence maximum and targeted a sixth-grade reading level. GPT-4o was used to critique and rank AI-generated summaries, and the two best-performing AI versions were compared with resident summaries. Blinded evaluations by three experienced nuclear medicine physicians assessed summaries on readability, accuracy, appropriateness, and overall fitness for purpose. Likelihood Ratio Chi-Square tests assessed differences in performance. ResultsGPT o1-mini was ranked as the best summary in 86% of initial AI comparisons and 100% of final comparative assessments with resident summaries. GPT 4o and o1-mini outperformed residents across multiple domains including clarity, health literacy, and tone. The best human summaries were consistently outperformed by AI in both physician and AI assessments, though discrepancies in ranking priorities (e.g., tolerance for jargon vs. inaccuracy) were noted and AI more often produced summaries containing misinterpretations of data in the original reports. Resident summaries showed wide variation in tone, technicality, and patient appropriateness. Overall, 65% of all summaries (AI and human) were deemed fit-for-purpose. ConclusionGenerative AI models can produce consistently appropriate and readable patient-facing summaries of imaging procedure reports and may serve as effective tools to develop resident communication skills. Generative AI may therefore model best practices and provide timely feedback, offering structured opportunities to refine written communication. Future work should explore its integration into learner-tailored educational constructs using frameworks such as Bloom’s taxonomy, to enhance resident training and effectiveness of feedback mechanisms.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Background Emerging artificial intelligence-based technologies are increasingly influencing teaching and learning practices in healthcare education, offering new opportunities for student engagement, learning, and skill development. Objective The purpose of this study was to explore utilization of artificial intelligence in audiology and speech-language pathology education based on insights from students. Further, to explore their awareness, use, perceived benefits, barriers, and attitudes toward the integration of artificial intelligence. Method A cross-sectional online survey of 17 questions was distributed to 483 audiology and speech-language pathology students enrolled in undergraduate, postgraduate and doctoral programmes across multiple institutions in India through social media platforms. The questionnaire was developed following a review of previously published studies examining students’ perceptions of the implications of artificial intelligence in education. Descriptive analysis was used to analyse the findings. Results A total of 286 students participated in the study (mean age = 21.73 ± 2.33 years), of whom 82.2% were females. Most participants (96.9%) were aware of artificial intelligence technologies, and 89.9% indicated using artificial intelligence tools for educational purposes. Regarding the future role of artificial intelligence in education, 75.1% disagreed that it could replace human lecturers. Students primarily used it for assignments and exam preparation, while limited institutional acceptance was a major barrier to its implementation. Conclusions Students expressed an optimistic view regarding the application of artificial intelligence in education. Students reported concerns about inaccurate artificial intelligence-generated information, while limited acceptance, inadequate knowledge, and ethical concerns hindered its effective integration into education.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract Research Summary We develop an ecosystem perspective on AI‐enabled value creation, grounded in AI's characteristics as a general‐purpose technology. We consider that AI can support multiple value propositions realized through distinct but interconnected ecosystems. Within this structure, AI innovators face choices concerning which value propositions to support, whether to pursue them through general‐purpose or specialized offers, and whether to make those offers open or closed. Users, in turn, are strategic actors facing choices among alternative ecosystem configurations of focal offers and complements through which the same value proposition might be realized. These choices by innovators and users may alter ecosystem roles and competitive relationships over time. We conclude by outlining research opportunities for strategy and innovation scholars examining how firms create and capture value in AI‐enabled ecosystems. Managerial Summary Value creation with AI depends not only on the technology's capability but on the actors whose combined contributions deliver a value proposition. AI supports many value propositions, each through its own ecosystem, with some elements shared across them. AI innovators choose which value propositions to serve, whether to do so through general‐purpose or specialized offers, and whether to make their offers open or proprietary. User firms choose among alternative configurations of offers and complements through which the same value proposition can be realized. These choices may shift the competitive relationships between actors within an ecosystem over time. This perspective surfaces questions of relevance for scholars and practitioners regarding value creation and capture with AI.

Road traffic crashes are among the major causes of preventable deaths in Kenya and public service vehicles (PSVs) make significant proportion of the serious crashes, especially long-distance buses. Vehicle inspection is a statutory obligation but the arrangements for vehicle maintenance vary between bus companies. This study aimed at establishing the relationship between the maintenance management practices and safety performance of the long-distance bus companies in Kenya. The study adopted a quantitative, cross-sectional, explanatory correlational design, based on the Systems Theory, Human Factors Theory and Safety Culture Theory. Structured questionnaires were used to gather information from the managers and drivers of licensed companies on the aforementioned corridors, 228 questionnaires were retrieved from the 325 questionnaires distributed (70.2%). Descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation and multiple linear regression were used to analyse the data in SPSS 28. The overall mean rating for the maintenance was 3.01, which is considered moderate. Maintenance was significantly correlated with safety performance (r = .254, p < .001), and it remained a significant predictor when fleet management, driver management, and transport planning and scheduling were controlled (B = 0.206, β = .207, t = 3.425, p = .001, 95% CI [0.088, 0.325]). The model explained 20.9% of the variance in safety performance (adjusted R² = .195), F(4, 223) = 14.722, p < .001, and the null hypothesis was rejected. Companies which maintained schedule for preventative maintenance, had routine vehicle checks, maintained a vehicle maintenance record, and made use of accredited workshops, had better safety performance. Maintenance should hence be seen as a fundamental safety activity in an integrated safety management system and should be addressed by bus companies and the regulator. Keywords: Vehicle Maintenance Management; Preventive Maintenance; Safety Performance; Long-Distance Buses

Humanity is transferring its accumulated knowledge to machines at extraordinary speed - yet the governance frameworks needed to constrain what those machines can do with that knowledge remain dangerously underdeveloped. This essay argues that the concentration of intellectual and operational power in AI systems poses a governance challenge distinct from conventional technology risk. When AI agents can multiply capabilities through networked cooperation, when safeguards are implemented in the same computational environment they are meant to govern, and when boundaries between separately owned systems fail to constrain emergent capabilities, the standard assumption of human oversight becomes increasingly difficult to sustain in practice. The essay examines four compounding vulnerabilities: the new concentration of power enabled by systems that can process and act on vast bodies of knowledge; the multiplication of capability when agents communicate and share discoveries; the erosion of organizational boundaries that were assumed to contain AI behavior; and the structural contradiction of software guardrails governing systems that may be able to circumvent them. Against this backdrop, the essay proposes a design principle with practical implications: the mandatory pause. Drawing on Ternary Logic - a framework built around three distinct states representing refusal (-1), unresolved conditions (0), and authorization (+1) - it argues that the authority to act must never follow automatically from the capability to act. For consequential operations, enforceable conditions must be satisfied before a system may proceed, through mechanisms that the acting system cannot unilaterally waive. The argument concludes that AI governance requires not promises of responsible behavior but architectures in which restraint is a verifiable property of the system itself - independently testable, resistant to circumvention, and answerable to society rather than to the institutions that built it.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Rare but severe failures of large language models can become practically significant at deployment scale. Estimating their probabilities with direct Monte Carlo sampling is highly inefficient, while proposal-based methods typically require auxiliary learning of an additional proposal distribution. We introduce \textbf{Weighted Ensemble (WE)}, a training-free framework for rare-event estimation in language models. WE samples exclusively from the original language model and improves upon direct Monte Carlo by periodically reallocating the sampling budget toward prefixes that appear more likely to reach the target rare event. To guide this reallocation without learning a separate proposal distribution, we exploit internal LLM representations as prefix-level signals and empirically validate their effectiveness. We provide a theoretical analysis of the proposed algorithm. Experiments on safety-related tasks spanning both small-scale and modern large-scale LLMs demonstrate that WE improves the efficiency and reliability of rare-event probability estimation.

Human-AI Interaction is commonly evaluated by what an artificial agent enables during use, yet interaction can also alter the human who acts next. We introduce Residual Human States, a trajectory-based framework for representing the potentially multidimensional human state carried forward after interaction with AI, relative to a relevant alternative trajectory. The framework distinguishes assisted output from human-state transition and derives four empirical propositions: multidimensionality, interaction-policy dependence, horizon dissociation, and temporal persistence. Its central claim is that assisted performance does not by itself determine the human state carried forward. We examine these propositions through four empirical cases with different inferential roles. Published medical-training evidence illustrates how one AI interaction history can be associated with both slightly higher observed accuracy on some later unaided cases and transmission of a systematic decision bias on others. A second diagnostic-learning study shows that later unaided behaviour differs across AI-support policies, while also revealing that aggregate accuracy cannot by itself distinguish improved discrimination from a shifted response criterion. In a classroom experiment, generative-AI tutoring substantially improved assisted practice performance without a corresponding detectable gain on a subsequent unaided exam. A longitudinal reanalysis of personalised AI dialogue further shows that residual contrasts can evolve across post-interaction horizons and that such change may arise from the comparison trajectory as well as from the focal intervention. Evaluating interactive AI systems therefore requires attention not only to contemporaneous performance, but also to which human states alternative interaction trajectories produce, relative to which counterfactuals, and how durably.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract Background Whilst the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare is growing, with promises that AI will reduce costs and improve efficiency, there is also concern that AI systems can perpetuate health inequalities. Prior work has explored patients’ trust in AI, but less attention has been given to how patients conceptualise the fairness of AI decision-making in healthcare and which factors influence these views. Methods We conducted a cross-sectional survey of UK patients, recruited through public and patient involvement and engagement (PPIE) networks, exploring perceptions of fairness across two AI vignettes: a patient-facing symptom checker and a clinician-facing cancer treatment decision-support tool. Respondents rated the perceived impact of 13 factors on the fairness of AI decisions and completed free-text responses to identify any additional factors. Demographics and survey variables were reported using descriptive statistics, along with Pearson’s chi-square test for differences in attitudes. Associations were estimated using ordinal logistic regression. Free-text responses were analysed thematically. Results A total of 149 respondents from the UK completed the survey. The factor perceived to most strongly undermine fairness of AI decisions was the absence of human supervision, with 89.9% of respondents reporting that AI decisions that could not be questioned by patients or clinicians would negatively impact fairness. This was followed by AI tools developed without clinician input (89.3%) and incorrect data in electronic health records (86.6%). Perceptions were consistent across both vignettes. Thematic analysis identified additional concerns not captured in the structured survey, including accessibility, the complexity of long-term conditions, ongoing maintenance of AI systems and the loss of human empathy. Conclusions Patients hold nuanced, wide-ranging concerns about fairness which span the AI lifecycle from development and deployment to maintenance. We offer design considerations, including the need for human-in-the-loop systems designed with end users and that can adapt to professional input, to support the development of fair AI systems in healthcare.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Generative AI is rapidly reshaping video advertising production. Using expectancy violations theory as an interpretive lens, this study develops a framework in which ad appeal (rational vs. emotional), product type (high-tech vs. low-tech), and AI character embodiment (no character vs. animal-like vs. human-like) jointly relate to ad attitude and to two appraisals: perceived novelty and perceived uncanniness. This study tests the framework in five between-subjects experiments with consumers recruited from an online panel. Results show that rational appeals outperform emotional appeals in AI-generated ads, especially for low-tech products. Novelty is positively and uncanniness negatively associated with ad attitude, and the indirect effects through both appraisals are consistent with the proposed process. Human-like AI characters amplify uncanniness in emotional low-tech executions. In one rational low-tech execution, an animal-like character lowered uncanniness relative to a no-character baseline, but ad attitude did not differ significantly. The findings extend expectancy-violation theorizing in AI advertising and offer configuration-level design guidance for brands deploying disclosed AI-generated advertising.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly transforming how tourists search for information, plan itineraries, and make travel decisions. However, limited qualitative research explains how tourists negotiate their agency when AI becomes actively involved in travel decision-making. This study explores how tourists experience GenAI-mediated travel decisions, focusing on autonomy, trust, skepticism, authenticity, and spontaneity. Drawing on a qualitative research approach, semi-structured interviews were conducted with six tourists who had experience using GenAI for travel planning. Thematic analysis identified five interconnected themes: AI as a travel decision partner; between convenience and decision autonomy; trust, verification, and skepticism; the tension between ai optimization and travel spontaneity; and reconstructing authenticity in AI-mediated travel. The findings indicate that tourists perceive GenAI as a decision partner rather than a replacement for human judgment. AI enhances planning convenience but can increase reliance, making autonomy a negotiated process. Trust is conditional and supported by verification, while AI optimization creates tensions with spontaneity. Furthermore, AI can facilitate authentic experiences while potentially contributing to algorithmic standardization. The study contributes to tourism research by conceptualizing AI-mediated travel decision-making as a process of negotiated agency between tourists and AI.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in instructional feedback processes in marketing education, yet little is known about how students psychologically process feedback when it is attributed to AI rather than a human instructor. To clarify the state of the field, we first conduct a systematic literature review of 25 peer-reviewed studies on AI use in higher education, revealing a dominance of technology adoption and performance-focused models and a limited integration of emotional and relational mechanisms in AI-mediated feedback contexts. Building on source credibility theory and affective appraisal perspectives, we then test a moderated serial mediation model using a 2 × 2 experiment with undergraduate marketing students (N = 371). Results show that feedback valence significantly influences positive emotional responses, and this effect is amplified when feedback is attributed to AI rather than to a human instructor. Emotional responses subsequently shape perceived feedback clarity, instructor likability, and perceived instructor benevolence, which in turn predict engagement intentions. The findings demonstrate that AI-generated feedback is not processed as a neutral delivery channel but as a socially interpreted evaluative source. By integrating systematic synthesis with experimental evidence, this study advances a process-oriented understanding of the emotional and relational consequences of AI-mediated feedback in marketing education.

Large language models (LLMs) reach users only after a chain of transfer steps: full or parameter-efficient fine-tuning, preference alignment, prompting, and changes to the decoding procedure. Each step alters the model, the distribution it faces, or both. Yet fairness and robustness are usually assessed once, on a single fixed test set. This paper presents a unified group-conditional framework to analyze how transfer affects the fairness and robustness of LLMs, and how existing methods try to preserve these properties. To characterize these trade-offs, we introduce a analytical framework that views fair and robust transfer as constrained distributionally robust optimization. We view fair and robust transfer as constrained distributionally robust optimization whose feasible set is determined by the transfer interface, and we split any change in a fairness gap into an update term, caused by changing the model, and shift term, caused by changing the data. Building on existing fairness-transfer bounds, we record two elementary consequences that the LLM literature has not made explicit: the group-conditional bound on the shift term is tight, and when only one group shifts, the marginal shift equals exactly a \( \pi_{\min} \) fraction of the fairness-relevant shift, where \( \pi_{\min} \) is that group's proportion. We use these observations to classify mitigation methods by interface and by the term they target, to offer a reading under which conflicting findings on low-rank adaptation are compatible, and to derive reporting recommendations. We close with open problems, including per-group certificates, fairness of approximate decoding, and cumulative drift under continual transfer.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Understanding facial behaviour in video requires answering three fundamental questions: when a key facial expression occurs, where the model attends on the face at that moment, and why that evidence is necessary rather than merely correlated. Today's multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can label and describe video, but they rarely provide faithful explanations, especially for small facial movements that change over time. We present VideoFace-X-LLM, a framework for explainable facial video understanding comprising two key components. First, we introduce ExplainFace, a weakly supervised video-text corpus for facial behaviour understanding, automatically constructed from CelebV-HQ videos and validated through human evaluation and a two-model audit (at most 2.3% contradictions), demonstrating consistent gains across two backbone architectures. Second, H-TCC (Hierarchical Temporal Spatial Causal Concepts), which finds the key temporal moments (When), the facial regions (Where), and verifies its causal necessity (Why) through targeted occlusion. Fine-tuning on ExplainFace raises appearance Macro F1 from 19.48% to 32.87% (+13.39), with gains of +4.38 on actions, +6.77 on temporal emotion, and +11.84 F1 on deepfake detection. We also measure the explanations pointing lift, face/edge lift, stability, an Adebayo sanity check, and a necessity test rather than only showing examples. Our models, code, and corpus are available on request for research use.

Model routing can reduce the cost of LLM applications by assigning simpler requests to cheaper models without sacrificing the quality of the response. However, most routers treat requests as independent. Stateful agents do not operate under this assumption: a user turn may require multiple model and tool calls, its difficulty depends on the state produced by earlier turns, and changing models can sacrifice reuse of the conversational prompt cache. We study zero-shot, cost-aware routing at the user-turn boundary, systematically varying the routing rule, access to session history, candidate models that differ in size, reasoning effort, or model provider, and prompt-cache behavior. We evaluate on multi-turn versions of SheetCopilot and SpreadsheetBench 2, where persistent workbooks and cross-turn dependencies make isolated routing decisions especially brittle. At a matched offloading rate, giving the router session history improves task pass rate over the same router without history, with gains for every model pair; history-aware routing remains within one point of always using the expensive model. We also found that cost depends on execution dynamics rather than token prices alone: the cheaper model's per-task cost advantage narrows from 6.8x to 3.2x on longer sessions. A closed form cache analysis further shows that downward switches (expensive to cheap) recover their cache cost within two LLM calls, whereas upward switches do not break even under the evaluated conditions. Together, these results show that agent routing is a sequential decision problem: effective policies must account for what happened earlier in the session and for the asymmetric cost of switching models.

OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to describe work-related traumatic brain injury (wrTBI) incidence among working-age Wisconsinites in the Wisconsin Trauma Registry (WTR). METHODS: Incident-level WTR data from 2017 to 2024 were analyzed by work-related and demographic factors. WrTBI incidence for demographics was assessed by chi-square analyses. Age-adjusted incidence rates (IR) were calculated by industry and occupation. RESULTS: Incidents of wrTBI were associated with older ages, when compared with other work-related injuries. Agriculture, Forestry, Fishing and Construction industries (and related occupational groups) had the highest rates of wrTBI. Transportation and Public Utilities, and Building and Grounds Cleaning and Maintenance Occupations, also had significantly elevated IRs. CONCLUSIONS: These findings support previous analyses while adding a novel finding for Building and Grounds Cleaning and Maintenance Occupations to the literature. Trauma registries are a rich source for occupational health surveillance.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Worker augmentation dominates current narratives about robotics and AI. These technologies may, however, also produce worker deaugmentation, which occurs when technology automates the tasks employees value most while leaving them responsible for lower-value, monotonous activities. This letter introduces worker deaugmentation, argues that it is particularly relevant in tourism and hospitality, where occupations combine diverse manual and cognitive tasks, and advances two propositions. We illustrate them in a back-of-the-house occupation, rating the 14 core tasks O*NET assigns to the cook occupation, evaluating each according to its subjective value and likelihood of automation. Expert assessments indicate that seven support the deaugmentation effect: five highly valued tasks are highly automatable, whereas two low-value tasks appear resistant to automation. These findings suggest that automation may reduce job quality and intrinsic motivation. A two-by-two framework distinguishes deaugmentation risk from beneficial automation and indicates where job design should intervene.
topics: Labor market dynamics and wage inequality

documents.abstract: Digital health technologies and artificial intelligence are transforming clinical workflows by automating documentation, inbox management, prior authorizations, and decision support tasks that have historically contributed to physician burnout. These innovations promise to reduce administrative burden and restore time for patient interaction, but they also introduce new forms of cognitive overload, including alert fatigue, click fatigue, and expectations of continuous availability. This chapter examines how the “invisible work” of care—coordination, communication, and documentation—has expanded in the electronic era and how automation may reshape these responsibilities. It explores both the benefits and unintended consequences of digital tools and proposes strategies for redesigning clinical workflows around human cognitive limits rather than technological capability. Understanding how to balance efficiency with well-being will determine whether artificial intelligence improves clinician experience or deepens burnout in increasingly complex healthcare environments.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

Sintetik medianing kognitiv yuklama (cognitive load), soxta xotira (false memory), "epistemik xavotir" (epistemic anxiety) hamda "yolgʻonchining dividendi" (liar's dividend) kabi psixologik fenomenlarni keltirib chiqarish mexanizmlari tizimlashtirilgan. Tadqiqotda ushbu kognitiv xatoliklar va kutilayotgan psixologik reaksiyalarning foizli taqsimoti Pie Chart (doiraviy diagramma) va uning statistik tahlili orqali modellashtirilgan.
