documents.abstract: Retail participation in India’s Futures and Options (F&O) market has grown rapidly, and AI-based trading tools are now widely available to individual traders, yet regulatory data indicate that most individual derivative traders incur net losses. Existing studies have largely examined why investors adopt AI tools and not whether adoption improves trading outcomes. This study examines the correlation between AI adoption and trading performance among retail F&O traders in six cities of Karnataka, with Trading Decision Quality as the mediating mechanism and Financial Literacy as the moderating condition. Data was gathered using a five-point Likert-scale questionnaire from 401 retail Foreign Exchange (F&O) traders and evaluate using Exploratory Factor Analysis (SPSS) and Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (SmartPLS, 5,000 bootstrap resamples). AI Adoption was identified as a construct consisting of three factors, namely, Perceived Usefulness and Continued Reliance, Perceived Ease of Use, and Trust in AI Reliability. It can be seen that AI Adoption has a positive impact on both Trading Decision Quality and Trading Performance. Trading Decision Quality acts as a partial mediator in the correlation between AI Adoption and Trading Performance, which means that the use of AI tools leads to favourable results by virtue of facilitating higher quality decisions while trading. Financial Literacy plays a positive moderating role in the influence of AI Adoption on Trading Performance, implying that traders with higher levels of financial literacy reap more advantages from AI tools. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence Adoption, Trading Decision Quality, Financial Literacy, Trading Performance, Retail F&O Traders

Rapid urbanization and persistent road-safety challenges have increased the demand for intelligent traffic management systems capable of supporting traffic monitoring, incident analysis, and short-term forecasting. Existing artificial intelligence solutions frequently address these functions through separate, task-specific applications, making it difficult for traffic operators to access heterogeneous analytical services within a common operational environment. This study presents a cloud-based, multi-source traffic intelligence platform that incorporates independent analytical services for CCTV video, UAV video, and IoT sensor data. The proposed platform performs platform-level service integration among the three sources. Its principal analytical component is a multi-model, multi-task UAV video framework consisting of three task-specific pipelines for accident detection and classification, emergency-vehicle detection, and vehicle tracking, counting, and congestion analysis. The semantic outputs of these pipelines are integrated at the decision level to generate annotated videos, traffic statistics, congestion assessments, incident alerts, and consolidated traffic reports. YOLOv8-based models are used for traffic-object and incident detection, Deep SORT is employed for multi-object tracking, and DCRNN is independently applied to PeMS-BAY sensor data for short-term traffic forecasting. A graph-partitioning strategy with overlapping boundary nodes is also evaluated to investigate the trade-off between forecasting accuracy and computational efficiency. Module-level experiments demonstrate effective task-specific performance. The CCTV accident detection model achieves a validation precision of 89.09%, recall of 88.10%, and mAP of 88.09%. The augmented UAV accident-analysis model achieves a validation precision of 82.20% and mAP of 80.20%. For five-minute traffic forecasting, the DCRNN service obtains an MAE of 0.85, MAPE of 1.63%, and RMSE of 1.54 on the PeMS-BAY dataset. These results demonstrate the feasibility of integrating independently processed traffic-analysis services within a common cloud platform while using multi-model UAV analytics to provide consolidated aerial traffic intelligence.

Conversational artificial intelligence (AI) has moved from novelty to infrastructure. Rulebased chatbots that once nudged users through smoking-cessation scripts have given way to large language model (LLM)-powered agents capable of open-ended, multilingual, empathetic-sounding dialogue, available around the clock at near-zero marginal cost. Systematic and scoping reviews now document measurable effects of AI chatbots on physical activity, diet, smoking cessation, medication adherence, and mental distress across thousands of participants (Feng et al., 2025). The World Health Organization (WHO) itself has deployed a generative AI assistant, S.A.R.A.H., to test population-scale health communication (van Kolfschooten et al., 2025). Taken together, these developments justify treating conversational AI not merely as a clinical or commercial curiosity, but as an emerging layer of public health infrastructure -one that sits alongside water systems, mass media, and vaccination programs as a determinant of how populations receive, interpret, and act on health information. (Wang et al., 2024). This opinion argues that the digital public health community should engage conversational AI on exactly those terms: as infrastructure, not gadgetry. Infrastructure framing changes the questions we ask. Instead of "does the chatbot work?" we should ask who it works for, under what governance, and with what consequences for equity, trust, and the broader information ecosystem. I organize this argument around three tensions that recur across the recent literature: (i) genuine behavioral efficacy versus fragile evidentiary depth; (ii) the promise of expanded access versus the risk of a new digital divide; and (iii) the communicative power of generative AI versus its capacity to manufacture and amplify misinformation. I close by proposing that Sustainable Development Goal (SDG)aligned public health institutions adopt a public-interest design standard for conversational AI, rather than leaving its trajectory to consumer technology markets alone.The evidence base for AI chatbots in health promotion has grown quickly and, on balance, positively. A widely cited systematic review found that AI chatbots produced favorable outcomes across lifestyle modification domains, particularly physical activity, diet, and smoking cessation (Aggarwal et al., 2023). A 2026 scoping review of 43 studies (Fu et al., 2026) reported that 82% of behavior-change comparisons trended positive, though only about a third reached moderate or larger effect sizes, and cost-effectiveness data were essentially absent. A meta-analysis focused on adolescents and young adults (Feng et al., 2025) similarly found chatbots effective for alleviating mental distress and supporting health behaviors, while noting substantial heterogeneity in intervention design and outcome measurement. Three limitations temper enthusiasm. First, most trials are short, nonclinical, adult-skewed, and rarely randomized at scale; only about a third of studies in the largest recent scoping review were randomized controlled trials (Fu et al., 2026). Second, "AI chatbot" spans an enormous range of systems, from rule-based decision trees to frontier LLMs, and pooling them obscures which architectural features actually drive behavior change (Kurniawan et al., 2024;Schachner et al., 2020). Third, almost no study reports durability beyond a few months, leaving open whether early engagement gains represent sustained health improvement or a novelty effect. For a section whose remit is population-level promotion and prevention rather than individual clinical outcomes, this matters: infrastructure decisions built on inflated short-term efficacy claims risk premature, poorly targeted public investment (Hampsher-Monk et al., 2024).A second tension concerns reach. Proponents rightly note that AI chatbots are inexpensive to scale, available in multiple languages, and can operate where clinical workforce is scarceattributes explicitly cited in WHO's own rationale for deploying S.A.R.A.H. as a research prototype for population health communication (Palmer & Schwan, 2025). Behavioralaccess frameworks extend this logic, arguing that digital health tools must be evaluated not only on availability but on whether populations can meaningfully engage with them across design, delivery, dissemination, and sustainment stages. Yet the same structural gaps that limit telemedicine and mobile health also constrain chatbot benefit: broadband access, device ownership, digital literacy, language coverage, and trust in institutional actors are unevenly distributed within and between countries (Banerjee, 2026). Chatbots trained and validated predominantly in high-resource, English-language settings may perform less reliably for populations with the greatest unmet need -the same populations digital public health is meant to prioritize under SDG 3, 9, and 11's emphasis on inclusive infrastructure and sustainable, resilient communities. A chatbot that reduces cost-per-contact for a health system does not automatically reduce disparities in outcomes; without equity-explicit design, deployment, and evaluation, it may simply reallocate existing advantages to those already best served by digital tools, echoing patterns already observed in AI-enabled primary care and telemedicine expansion (Elangovan et al., 2025).The third tension is the sharpest. The same generative capacity that lets an AI chatbot deliver personalized, conversational health guidance also lets it generate fluent, plausible-sounding health misinformation, and do so faster than human fact-checkers can respond. A 2025 opinion piece in this journal warned that generative AI tools function as de facto triage systems and informal health advisors in low-and middle-income countries, where their fluency can be mistaken for authority even when their outputs are unreliable. A parallel systematic review of generative AI and health misinformation catalogued mechanisms of production, propagation, and mitigation across text, image, and synthetic media, underscoring that the problem is not hypothetical but already observed at scale (Saeidnia et al., 2026). Mitigation research is advancing in step. Retrieval-augmented generation has been used to improve the factual reliability of LLM-based COVID-19 fact-checking tools (Li et al., 2025), and thematic-analysis pipelines have been proposed to detect and "inoculate" audiences against circulating misinformation narratives (Malek et al., 2026). A recent risk taxonomy specifically for public health LLM adoption (Zhou et al., 2025) offers a structured way for practitioners to reason about failure modes before deployment rather than after. Conversational AI for vaccine communication, an earlier and instructive precedent, showed both promise for addressing hesitancy and clear risk of amplifying inaccurate claims when systems were insufficiently curated (Passanante et al., 2023). The lesson across this literature is consistent: the communicative power of conversational AI is not neutral infrastructure like a water pipe; it actively shapes the epistemic environment it operates in, for better or worse, depending on design choices made well upstream of any individual conversation.Evidence highlights Population-level implication Efficacy vs. evidentiary depth ~82% of behavior-change comparisons favorable, but only ~1/3 with moderate+ effect sizes; RCTs a minority (Fu et al., 2026) provenance, and risk taxonomies (Zhou et al., 2025) prior to releaseNone of this argues against conversational AI in public health; the direction of the evidence is cautiously positive, and the WHO's own experimentation with S.A.R.A.H. reflects institutional recognition that this technology will be used regardless of academic ambivalence. The argument is instead for treating conversational AI the way public health has learned, sometimes painfully, to treat other infrastructure: as a shared resource whose design choices carry population-level consequences, and which therefore warrants governance commensurate with its reach. Three concrete commitments follow. First, funders and health systems evaluating AI chatbot interventions should require reporting of architecture (rulebased versus LLM-based, retrieval-augmented or not), population stratification by digitalaccess indicators, and effect durability beyond the intervention period -the absence of which currently limits comparability across the field (Fu et al., 2026). Second, deployment in low-resource or multilingual settings should be preceded by equity-focused validation rather than assumed from high-resource pilot data, consistent with behavioral-access frameworks that treat dissemination and sustainment as distinct design stages, not afterthoughts. Third, any public health-facing conversational agent should be built on retrieval-grounded, provenance-transparent architectures and evaluated against a structured risk taxonomy before release, rather than relying on post hoc misinformation cleanup. WHO's 2024 guidance on large multimodal models already articulates comparable principles -transparency, accountability, and human oversight -for governments and developers; the task now is operationalizing them at the level of individual chatbot deployments rather than treating them as abstract commitments.The digital public health field has an opportunity, still open but narrowing, to shape how conversational AI is integrated into population health promotion before deployment patterns harden into path dependency. The evidence reviewed here suggests genuine, if still shallow, behavioral benefit; genuine, if unevenly distributed, gains in access; and genuine, dual-use communicative power that can either strengthen or corrode public trust in health information depending on how it is engineered and governed. Framing conversational AI as infrastructure rather than as a discrete clinical tool has practical consequences: it shifts evaluation from short efficacy trials toward equity-stratified, durability-tested, misinformation-resilient deployment standards, and it shifts responsibility from individual developers toward the institutions, including public health agencies, research funders, and journals such as this one, that decide what counts as sufficient evidence for scale. A reasonable objection is that infrastructure-level governance risks slowing beneficial innovation, particularly in settings where any accessible health guidance outperforms none. That concern is legitimate and argues for proportionate, tiered oversight rather than uniform restriction -lighter validation for low-stakes wellness nudges, more rigorous requirements for agents addressing vaccine hesitancy, chronic disease self-management, or crisis-adjacent mental health support. What the evidence does not support is treating conversational AI's current trajectory as selfcorrecting. Left to consumer technology incentives alone, generative health chatbots are likely to continue optimizing for engagement and fluency rather than for population-level epidemiological benefit or equitable reach. The digital public health community is well positioned, through funding priorities, publication standards, and partnership with bodies like WHO, to redirect that trajectory toward public-interest design before it further consolidates around existing digital and geographic advantage.

documents.abstract: Criminal networks increasingly exploit social media to organize, recruit, incite, and coordinate unlawful activities, whereas law-enforcement monitoring in Kenya remains largely manual and English-centric. This study aimed to design, implement, and rigorously evaluate an artificial intelligence (AI) ensemble framework for open-source intelligence (OSINT) classification of crime- and threat-relevant content in Kenya's trilingual (English, Kiswahili, and Sheng) and code-switched digital environment. A corpus of 6,212 documents was assembled from six sources: Twitter/X, Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, and two Sheng-language corpora. The corpus was weakly labelled using a 214-term trilingual crime-and-threat lexicon. Label noise was quantified against a manually annotated stratified validation sample (n = 320), yielding Cohen's κ = 0.350, silver-label precision of 0.525, and recall of 0.750. Combined word- and character-level term frequency-inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) features comprising 25,831 dimensions were used to train a hyperparameter-tuned, weighted soft-voting ensemble consisting of multinomial naive Bayes, a calibrated linear support vector machine, random forest, logistic regression, and XGBoost. The decision threshold was calibrated using cross-validated out-of-fold probabilities. The optimized ensemble achieved 98.3% accuracy, 80.6% precision, 62.5% recall, 70.4% F1-score, 0.907 ROC-AUC, 0.724 PR-AUC, 0.702 Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC), and a 0.50% false-positive rate. The ensemble outperformed the best single learner and a frozen multilingual transformer baseline (F1 = 26.2%). Ablation analysis demonstrated the contribution of the Sheng-normalization layer, while comparison of class-imbalance strategies showed that cost-sensitive learning combined with threshold calibration produced the strongest overall performance compared with SMOTE-based resampling. The findings demonstrate that linguistically inclusive classical machine-learning ensembles can provide an accurate, auditable, and computationally deployable approach to proactive social-media crime prevention in low-resource, code-switched settings. The study also derives policy implications concerning threshold-calibrated triage, expert annotation, data-protection impact assessments, and safeguards against dual-use misuse.

Fitness applications usually record one behaviour in isolation, and large-language-model (LLM) coaches produce fluent advice whose numbers are rarely checked. This paper presents AI Fitness OS, a web application that keeps training, nutrition, hydration, sleep, weight, steps and goals in one per-user record, computes every numerical target deterministically from published equations and stated heuristics, and passes those targets to Google Gemini as binding constraints; each generated meal plan is re-checked in code against a ±5 % tolerance. The premise was examined through secondary research on a public dataset of 2,111 records, and the artefact through tests, simulation and live measurement. All eight lifestyle metrics that the system tracks or addresses were significantly associated with obesity level (Bonferroni-adjusted α = 0.00625), although only three remained so on 515 records resembling the original survey. A Random Forest that combined the eight metrics reached a macro-F1 of 0.720 against 0.263 for the best single metric (Wilcoxon W = 55, p = 0.00098). Across 1,000 simulated user profiles, every constrained meal plan fell within ±5 % of its calorie target, against 75 of 1,000 unconstrained plans (exact McNemar p < 10⁻²⁰⁰). The calculator agreed with the dataset's weight-category labels for 98.82 % of records, and live responses took 2.5–6.1 s at no cost. The findings support computing arithmetic, generating language and checking the output against the computed numbers.

The rapid expansion of solar energy has accelerated the adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) to improve forecasting accuracy, photovoltaic performance, intelligent control, fault diagnosis, energy storage management, and smart grid operation. Recent advances in machine learning, deep learning, Digital Twins, Physics-Informed Machine Learning, Edge AI, Federated Learning, and Generative AI have transformed solar energy systems into more adaptive and data-driven infrastructures. Despite these advances, challenges related to data quality, model generalization, computational efficiency, cybersecurity, and explainability continue to limit large-scale deployment. An integrated perspective is presented by connecting AI applications across photovoltaic systems, solar thermal technologies, energy storage, and intelligent energy networks within a unified renewable energy ecosystem. Emerging research trends and future directions highlight the evolution toward AI-native energy systems that support efficient, resilient, and sustainable intelligent societies.

The renewable energy is being transformed by Artificial Intelligence (AI) to create smarter, efficient, and adaptive wind systems. AI forecasts the wind using machine learning and neural networks and optimizes the performance of turbines and minimizes costs related to maintenance using predictive analytics. These inventions assist the operators in predicting the changes, setting the turbines, and reducing downtime. Urban deployment of AI facilitates the seamless synchronization of mass-scaled wind energy with smart grids as well as the systems of IoT. It balances loads dynamically, for instance, it trades energy in real time and improves stability in the grid. Heavy reliance on fossil fuels and extensive reliance on carbon emissions and fossil fuels can be reduced through the implementation of AI-driven systems that enhance energy efficiency, reliability, and sustainability through the integration of renewable sources, storage, and intelligent control.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming the wind energy sector, marking a major step toward sustainable and intelligent societies. As global energy demands rise and carbon reduction becomes urgent, AI offers powerful tools to enhance the efficiency, reliability, and scalability of wind power systems. Through technologies such as machine learning, deep learning, digital twins, and predictive analytics, AI optimizes turbine design, predictive maintenance, load forecasting, and smart grid integration. By leveraging big data from sensors, meteorological sources, and operational parameters, AI enables accurate wind prediction, timely fault detection, and real-time performance optimization. Additionally, AI-driven systems play an emerging role in urban wind integration by improving micro-wind utilization, energy storage, and distributed generation within smart cities. The chapter also addresses economic feasibility, environmental sustainability, and ethical implications of AI-enabled wind energy applications.

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has prompted rapidly growing body of scholarship on the role in chemistry education since the public release of ChatGPT in the late of 2022. This thematic narrative review synthesizes 40 English-language sources including empirical studies, curriculum reports, and stakeholder surveys, and systematic/bibliometric reviews published between 2020 and 2026, identified through a structured, author-curated search of recent chemistry-education and analytical-chemistry literature (see Methodology). Sources were coded inductively and organized into six recurring themes: AI/ML literacy as curriculum content; AI-driven tutoring, personalization, and accessibility; empirical evaluations of generative AI's chemical reasoning; stakeholder perceptions; AI's transformation of chemistry research and scientific communication; and equity, ethics, and systemic barriers. Across the reviewed literature, a recurring position though not a formal consensus is that AI should support rather than replace human instruction. Empirical evaluations consistently report that large language models generate fluent but sometimes hallucinated or subtly incorrect chemistry content, particularly for visual and multi-representational reasoning tasks. The corpus is concentrated in higher education and high-income countries, and this pattern should be interpreted as a prominent tendency in the reviewed literature rather than a field-wide finding. Priorities for chemistry educators include critical AI literacy instruction, assessment redesign, teacher professional development, and explicit attention to equity.

documents.abstract: Generative AI has significantly reduced the effort and expense of developing and refining venture ideas, without eliminating the uncertainty and resource limitations of executing a venture. This research examines the potential of AI-assisted business ideation (AIBI) to drive behavioral change in accessing entrepreneurial support infrastructure. The study uses technology-cognition-institutional framework to examine the relationship between AIBI and perceived feasibility (PF) and entrepreneurial consultancy services engagement (ECS) and how these two variables mediate the relationship between AIBI and entrepreneurial intentions (EI). The study analyzed data from 319 university students in Pakistan using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). It evaluated the reliability and validity of the measurement model and examined structural relationships through bootstrapping with bias-corrected confidence intervals. Findings indicate that AI-based business ideation positively affects perceived feasibility, which in turn enhances engagement with entrepreneurial creative strategies (ECS).Moreover, ECS positively and significantly affect entrepreneurial intention, this in turn has a positive and significant direct effect on AIBI. The pathway from AIBI to perceived feasibility to engagement in entrepreneurial consultancy services to entrepreneurial intention is significant, emphasizing that AIBI affects entrepreneurial intention both cognitively and institutionally. This study extends AI entrepreneurship research by showing that AI's effects on entrepreneurial intention go beyond boosting entrepreneurial cognition. This study also contributes to existing intention models by conceptualizing entrepreneurial consultancy services as an endogenous behavioral mediator rather than a contextual condition, offering a more complete explanation of AI-enabled ideation's role in entrepreneurial readiness.

Network intrusion detection is an important cybersecurity function because network traffic can contain benign activity as well as malicious behavior. This paper presents an AI-based Network Intrusion Detection System (AI-NIDS) that combines live packet capture, flow generation, machine-learning classification, explainable artificial intelligence, and web-based visualization. The prototype is implemented in an Ubuntu virtual machine hosted through VirtualBox. Scapy captures traffic visible on the virtual network interface, and related packets are grouped into flows. Four features that can be derived directly from live traffic—destination port, packet count, total bytes, and average packet size—are used by the live classification pipeline. CICIDS2017 is used for model training and evaluation. Isolation Forest is used for anomaly-oriented analysis, while Random Forest and XGBoost perform multi-class classification. SHAP provides feature-level explanations, and a Flask dashboard presents live flows, detections, and explanations. On a held-out test set of 22,339 samples, Random Forest achieved 90.67% accuracy and XGBoost achieved 94.42% accuracy; macro F1 scores were 0.78 and 0.81, respectively. The results demonstrate the feasibility of combining machine learning and explainability in a practical NIDS prototype, while highlighting limitations related to reduced live features, rare attack classes, false positives, and virtualized network scope.
topics: Internet Traffic Analysis and Secure E-voting

documents.abstract: The lack of access to finance is a major issue for young entrepreneurs, especially those who have poor credit scores, lack financial statements and have no collateral. Artificial intelligence (AI) based credit scoring systems have been seen as a potential solution to credit assessment using alternative data, but there are concerns about fairness, transparency, accountability and algorithmic exclusion. This study aims to understand the impact of AI-powered credit scoring on financial justice for young entrepreneurs in Dhaka City, focusing on perceptions of financial access, AI-driven lending opportunities, ethical concerns, and responsible decision-making practices. The study uses a qualitative research approach and thematic analysis to explore the experiences and perspectives of entrepreneurs on traditional credit assessment systems and AI-powered lending mechanisms. The results show that AI-powered credit scoring is seen as a potential means to financial inclusion, as it can include alternative data like digital transaction records and business activity data. But there are also important issues of algorithmic bias, data quality, privacy, transparency, and the risk of leaving out people with small digital footprints, participants note. The study also shows that in the context of AI-driven lending, financial justice encompasses not merely the opportunity to obtain a loan, but also procedural fairness, transparency or explain ability, accountability, and the ability to object to or challenge automated decisions. The study adds to the literature on responsible AI and financial inclusion by offering a socio-technical approach that combines technological innovation and human-centered governance. The results indicate that AI-based credit scoring can contribute to inclusive entrepreneurial finance if applied in an ethically guided, transparent, and accountable manner with proper human supervision.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: India is embedding artificial intelligence (AI) in public administration at the very moment its legal architecture for data protection, transparency and AI oversight is being rewritten. Between November 2025 and August 2026, the government issued the India AI Governance Guidelines, notified the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Rules 2025, hosted the AI Impact Summit, and began defending in the Supreme Court a constitutional challenge to the DPDP Act's amendment of the Right to Information (RTI) Act. This paper asks whether administrative efficiency, transparency, accountability and data protection can be reconciled in AI-driven governance in India. Using doctrinal analysis, policy analysis and a case study of Telangana's Samagra Vedika welfare-profiling system, it argues that the four values are not inherently opposed. The tensions arise from design choices, thin institutional capacity and broad exemptions for the State. The paper identifies four structural gaps: voluntary AI guidance without enforceable duties; consent-free State processing and wide exemptions under the DPDP Act; the narrowing of the RTI public-interest test; and the absence of a right to human review and explanation. It proposes a proportionality-based, risk-tiered framework combining statutory authorisation, impact assessments, algorithm registers, meaningful human review, independent audit and accessible redress. Legal positions are stated as at 28 September 2026.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Emerging zoonoses, particularly vector-borne ones, are driven by climate change, biodiversity loss and land-use change. Surveillance, however, remains fragmented and largely reactive, and often fails to detect the risk signals that precede spillover. This narrative review examines how artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML), integrated with georeferenced and climatic data, could support a transition toward predictive, anticipatory One Health surveillance. Using tick-borne encephalitis (TBE) and Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever (CCHF) as case studies, we distinguish evidence from conventional statistical models, ML models and deep-learning applica-tions. ML models combining climatic, land-cover and host variables have shown promising ret-rospective performance in mapping tick habitat suitability and TBE and CCHF risk, whereas deep learning has been applied mainly to tick identification. However, AI evidence specific to TBE and CCHF remains limited: few disease-specific studies exist, validation is largely internal, no model has been evaluated prospectively, and some reported figures derive from synthetic data. We consider this gap a key finding. We also discuss data quality, model transferability, validation practices, al-gorithmic transparency and the EU AI Act. AI may enable a shift from costly emergency response toward validated Early Warning Systems if methodological, infrastructural and regulatory gaps are addressed. We outline priorities for researchers, veterinarians, clinicians and policymakers.

Autonomous Underwater Vehicles (AUVs), commonly known as submarine drones, provide a critical capability for modern naval operations requiring persistent presence in contested and GPS denied environments. This paper addresses autonomous positioning and area keeping of AUVs within predefined underwater zones using integrated inertial, acoustic, and velocity based navigation systems. Artificial intelligence techniques, including machine learning–based sensor fusion and adaptive decision making, enhance state estimation, navigation robustness, and control performance in uncertain and dynamic environments. By combining AI enabled perception with robust control algorithms, AUVs can maintain precise station keeping and boundary awareness while compensating for ocean currents and environmental disturbances. These capabilities support force protection, intelligence gathering, and undersea surveillance missions, enabling discreet and sustained operations with minimal human intervention.

Chemical manufacturers and distributors are increasingly dependent upon a steady stream of data from sensors, lab systems, logistics platforms and connected assets. However, when records are fragmented, unverifiable, or difficult to exchange across organisational boundaries, lifecycle decisions remain exposed to avoidable uncertainty. This review examines the integration of artificial intelligence, blockchain, and the Industrial Internet of Things within a trusted data architecture for the chemical lifecycle in Saudi Arabia. A structured integrative review synthesised peer-reviewed studies mainly published between 2020 and 2025 on industrial IoT security, edge intelligence, blockchain provenance, federated learning, digital twins, smart-contract governance, and supply chain traceability. The evidence indicates that no single technology resolves the trust problem in isolation. Artificial intelligence can spot anomalous or implausible process data, but its outputs inherit the weaknesses of the data pipeline. Blockchain can preserve event provenance and enforce multi-party rules, but high-frequency telemetry should not be directly stored on-chain. The IoT offers operational visibility but the attack surface is expanded by heterogeneous devices, legacy protocols, and weak identities. The review therefore develops a layered architecture where raw telemetry resides in governed off-chain stores, critical lifecycle events are hashed and signed to a permissioned consortium ledger, and edge or federated intelligence provides validation, anomaly detection, predictive functions, and decision support. The proposed design offers auditable event commitments that tie feedstock receipt, processing, quality release, storage, transport, downstream handoff and recovery. For organisations operating in Saudi Arabia's chemical industry, identity governance, semantic interoperability, latency-aware partitioning, privacy-preserving analytics, accountable smart contracts, and phased integration with existing operational technology are central implementation priorities. The review concludes that trusted lifecycle management is less about maximising blockchain usage and more about allocating a narrow, verifiable role for each technology within an end-to-end governance model.

documents.abstract: The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), biometric recognition, intelligent transportation systems, distributed energy platforms, and connected vehicles has resulted in increasingly heterogeneous digital infrastructures. Although these systems generate substantial quantities of data and provide sophisticated analytical capabilities, their effectiveness is frequently constrained by fragmented architectures, incompatible data representations, isolated databases, security vulnerabilities, and inadequate mechanisms for trusted information exchange. Interoperability has therefore emerged as a fundamental requirement for the development of intelligent digital ecosystems. However, interoperability cannot be treated exclusively as a technical problem because data integration also involves organizational, semantic, institutional, privacy, security, and governance considerations. This paper investigates the relationship between AI and interoperability and develops a conceptual socio-technical framework for integrating heterogeneous intelligent systems. The study synthesizes research concerning machine-learning-based face recognition, electronic toll collection, peer-to-peer energy trading, human-bot discrimination, federated intrusion detection, low-code/no-code intelligent automation, and secure computing. Particular attention is given to data classification, standardization, semantic compatibility, data friction, privacy-preserving computation, and secure AI deployment. The analysis demonstrates that AI can improve interoperability through intelligent classification, entity matching, anomaly detection, prediction, and automated decision support. Conversely, interoperable infrastructures can improve AI by providing access to more diverse and contextually relevant information. Nevertheless, increasing interoperability can also amplify privacy risks, surveillance capabilities, security threats, algorithmic bias, and unauthorized secondary use of data. The proposed framework consequently combines data and semantic interoperability with AI services, security controls, privacy-preserving mechanisms, governance, and continuous evaluation. The paper concludes that successful AI-enabled interoperability requires a balanced approach in which technical integration is accompanied by standardized representations, privacy-by-design, decentralized learning where appropriate, secure interfaces, transparent governance, and continuous performance assessment.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Vestibular disorders are common, heterogeneous, and diagnostically challenging. Nystagmus is an important sign in vestibular assessment, but its interpretation can depend on clinician expertise and recording quality. This structured narrative review mapped current evidence on artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled nystagmus and eye-movement signal analysis in vestibular assessment, focusing on study characteristics, input data, AI tasks, model architectures, validation approaches, performance metrics, explainability, and clinical applicability. A structured PubMed search identified human studies that developed, validated, or evaluated machine-learning, deep-learning, or related computational methods for nystagmus analysis or vestibular diagnostic support. Fifteen studies were included, most published from 2021 onwards. The evidence was dominated by technical and early-stage model-development studies using VNG/VOG recordings, other eye-movement recordings, or derived features such as pupil trajectories, optical-flow maps, eye and head traces, and slow-phase velocity measures. Applications included nystagmus detection, pupil tracking and signal extraction, pattern or direction classification, quantification or localisation, and benign paroxysmal positional vertigo-related diagnostic classification. Deep-learning approaches, particularly convolutional neural networks and CNN-recurrent hybrid models, were commonly used. However, validation was mainly internal, performance reporting was heterogeneous, explainability was limited, and prospective workflow evaluation or routine clinical implementation was uncommon. AI-enabled nystagmus analysis shows promising clinical potential, particularly for VNG/VOG-based assessment and BPPV-related decision support. Translation into routine practice will require multicentre patient-level external validation, transparent reporting, interpretable outputs, standardised performance metrics, and prospective evaluation in real clinical pathways.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in the social sciences to simulate human behavior and communication, yet validation methods for these applications remain limited. Existing evaluations often rely on human judgments of plausibility, a coarse, difficult-to-scale, and often unreliable benchmark for distinguishing AI-generated from human text. As a result, researchers lack robust tools for assessing the realism of LLM-generated language and for calibrating models to real-world data. We address this gap in two ways. First, we introduce the Conversational Human Authenticity Test (CHAT), a validation framework that combines aggregate metrics of detectability and semantic similarity with interpretable linguistic features, including stylistic markers and topical patterns, to assess how closely LLMs approximate human language in a given dataset. Second, we benchmark nine open-weight LLMs across five calibration strategies, including fine-tuning, stylistic prompting, and context retrieval, on user interactions from X, Bluesky, and Reddit. We find that even after calibration, LLM outputs remain clearly distinguishable from human text, especially in affective tone and emotional expression. Instruction-tuned models generally underperform base models, and larger models do not obviously improve human-likeness. We also identify a trade-off between realism and semantic fidelity: methods that make outputs seem more human often move them further from the content of human responses. Together, these results provide a scalable framework for validation and calibration in LLM-based social simulation while underscoring current limits in reproducing human communication.

Artificial intelligence is becoming embedded in organisational communication through message generation, conversational agents, monitoring systems, decision support, and automated service recovery. During crises, these functions offer speed, scale, consistency, and continuous availability, but they also change how stakeholders infer agency, competence, care, responsibility, and authenticity. This critical narrative review integrates crisis communication, organisational trust, human–automation trust, artificial intelligence-mediated communication, public relations, and service-recovery research to examine when AI-mediated communication is likely to sustain or erode stakeholder trust. The evidence indicates that no uniform ‘AI effect’ exists. Stakeholder responses depend on whether AI assists a human communicator or appears to replace one, whether the task is informational or relational, whether the crisis demands empathy and moral accountability, whether AI involvement is disclosed, and whether human responsibility remains visible. Technical or process transparency can strengthen perceived accountability and system trust, while simple disclosure that a message was produced with AI may reduce perceived legitimacy, authenticity, or credibility in some contexts. Anthropomorphic cues can increase social presence and perceived empathy, yet they may also raise expectations that become costly when the system fails. Evidence from crisis-response experiments, organisational studies, chatbot research, and service recovery therefore favours calibrated human–AI orchestration over indiscriminate automation. The review proposes that trustworthy AI-mediated crisis communication requires fit among task, crisis responsibility, stakeholder vulnerability, disclosure purpose, system reliability, and accountable human oversight. Current confidence is constrained by a literature dominated by short-term experiments, consumer and convenience samples, hypothetical crises, and limited longitudinal or field evidence. Research should move towards preregistered factorial studies, live crisis simulations, cross-cultural and multi-stakeholder designs, longitudinal trust measurement, and explicit testing of governance and escalation arrangements.

Education is becoming increasingly digital, yet many students still face difficulties in understanding complex concepts, remembering long answers, identifying their learning gaps, and preparing effectively for examinations. This paper presents an AI-powered adaptive learning platform designed to provide personalized and interactive learning support. The system uses Artificial Intelligence to explain questions in detail, generate short exam-oriented answers and recall keywords, analyze students' performance, identify knowledge gaps, and recommend suitable learning tasks. The platform also provides 3D visualization for mathematical and geometric concepts, AI-assisted learning for languages such as Marathi and Sanskrit with Hindi and English explanations, AI-based viva examination, instant tests, PDF/notes-based learning, progress tracking, and gamification. The main aim is to make learning personalized, understandable, interactive, and focused on actual student improvement rather than simply providing answers
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: The integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into higher education has precipitated a dual crisis: the exponential increase in faculty workload regarding assessment scalability and the destabilization of traditional academic integrity verification methods. This paper introduces the proposed system, an automated academic evaluation platform designed to address these challenges through a unified, immutable assessment pipeline. Unlike traditional Learning Management Systems (LMS) that function primarily as repositories, the proposed system employs Large Language Models (LLMs) to automate the entire grading lifecycle, from submission to feedback generation, while simultaneously performing rigorous authorship verification. The system enforces a single-submission policy to streamline administrative workflows and generates immutable, audit-ready reports containing scoring rationale and AIgenerated content likelihood. The system architecture, scoring methodology, and a multi-layered integrity detection approach based on stylometry and machine learning classifiers are described. Simulated performance results suggest that the proposed system mitigates the subjective variability of human grading while offering a scalable solution to the integrity challenges posed by unrestricted GenAI access.

Non-revenue water (NRW) — water produced and entering a distribution network but lost before it generates revenue — remains one of the most persistent inefficiencies in urban water management, with global losses estimated at roughly 126 billion cubic meters and USD 39 billion annually. Two technological families have been proposed, largely separately, to address this problem. Artificial intelligence (AI), through machine-learning and deep-learning models applied to pressure, flow, and acoustic data, improves the detection, localization, and prediction of leaks. Blockchain, a form of distributed ledger technology, offers a complementary capability: securing metering data, automating billing through smart contracts, and making reported consumption and loss figures auditable across multiple institutional stakeholders. This chapter argues that these two technologies address different parts of the same problem — AI improves analytical capability, while blockchain improves the trustworthiness of the data analyzed — and that treating them as substitutes rather than complements understates their combined potential. Building on this premise, the chapter develops a conceptual, three-layer architecture integrating an IoT-based data-acquisition layer, an AI analytics layer for leak detection and predictive maintenance, and a blockchain layer for data integrity and institutional trust, with a digital twin emerging as an integration concept rather than a separate technological layer. The framework is illustrated with reference to Türkiye’s regulatory context and to Gaziantep Su ve Kanalizasyon İdaresi (GASKİ), a metropolitan water and sewerage administration that reduced its reported NRW rate from above 49 percent in 2014 to approximately 25 percent in 2025, a trajectory its own management attributes partly to AI-integrated SCADA systems and precision pressure management. The chapter reviews pilot-level and early operational evidence for both technologies, distinguishes peer-reviewed findings from preprint and vendor material, and acknowledges that empirical support remains considerably stronger for AI-based leak management than for blockchain integration at utility scale. It concludes that public utilities facing legal and financial accountability for reported performance should prioritize reliable metering and AI-based analytics first, while testing blockchain in a single, high-value governance use case such as contractor-performance verification, and proposes a research agenda comparing otherwise similar systems with and without blockchain-based integrity assurance.

Advances in digital transformation, Industry 4.0, and big data technologies are fundamentally changing the competitive landscape in which businesses operate and reshaping traditional decision-making processes. Artificial intelligence, which lies at the heart of this technological transformation, not only automates business processes but also elevates them to a strategic level through its high data processing speed, continuous learning capabilities, and advanced predictive capabilities. Management accounting, which lies at the heart of businesses’ financial and strategic data flows, is significantly affected by this transformation. Artificial intelligence technologies are helping management accounting evolve beyond its traditional functions of data collection, processing, and reporting toward a more analytical and predictive framework. This transformation is opening up new possibilities in various management accounting practices, such as cost management, performance evaluation, financial forecasting, and the analysis of resource utilization. In particular, artificial intelligence’s advanced analytical capabilities enable managers to assess the company’s current situation more comprehensively and respond more quickly to changing conditions. Thus, the role of management accounting within the organization is evolving into a more active structure that goes beyond the presentation of financial information regarding past periods to generate forward-looking information and support strategic decision-making processes. The purpose of this study is to examine the impact of artificial intelligence technologies on management accounting and decision-making processes. The integration of artificial intelligence technologies into management accounting is driving transformation in various application areas, such as cost management, performance evaluation, and financial forecasting. To make effective use of artificial intelligence technologies, it is necessary to take into account factors such as data quality, data security and privacy, technological infrastructure, ethical principles, organizational conditions, and employees’ digital competencies. In addition, it is evident that artificial intelligence has not completely replaced human expertise in management accounting; human expertise remains important, particularly in activities that require professional judgment, interpretation, and strategic decision-making. For this reason, artificial intelligence is viewed not as a technology that replaces management accountants, but as a complementary tool that supports their analytical and strategic roles. In conclusion, the integration of artificial intelligence into management accounting can help businesses use data more effectively, support decision-making processes, and strengthen the strategic role of management accounting. In future research, it will be important to determine how management accounting tasks can be shared between humans and artificial intelligence, and in which tasks professional expertise and judgment will remain essential.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in criminal justice systems to improve efficiency and consistency, but its use in sentencing raises important questions about fairness, transparency, and judicial discretion. This article examines Malaysia’s introduction of AI-assisted sentencing through the Artificial Intelligence in Court Sentencing (AiCOS) system and asks how algorithmic assistance reshapes the exercise and visibility of sentencing discretion. It adopts a qualitative, desk-based, and interdisciplinary approach, drawing on criminology, legal and sociolegal scholarship, judicial and institutional materials, and international AI governance frameworks. The Malaysian experience is examined through four dimensions: transparency and explainability, procedural contestability, human discretion, and accountability, with comparative reference to the United States’s experience with COMPAS (Correctional Offender Management Profiling for Alternative Sanctions) and the European Union’s regulatory framework. The article argues that AiCOS is best understood not as an autonomous ‘AI judge’, but as an automated evolution of Malaysia’s existing Table of Sentencing . While its guidance function remains broadly similar, algorithmic mediation changes the visibility and contestability of the basis upon which punishment is determined. Automation therefore does not eliminate discretion but may relocate it into less visible decisions concerning data, system design, deployment, and reliance on algorithmic recommendations. The article concludes that retaining a human judge as the final decision-maker is insufficient, by itself, to ensure fairness. Effective governance requires transparency, disclosure, meaningful opportunities to challenge algorithmic inputs and recommendations, reasoned judicial decision-making, and continuing independent oversight.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become a central instrument of contemporary marketing, particularly in the form of algorithmic personalization of offers, messages and recommendations. While the literature in advanced economies documents both the commercial value of personalization and the consumer resistance it can provoke, emerging digital markets remain comparatively underexplored. This conceptual paper develops an integrative framework that explains how the quality of AI-driven personalization translates into purchase intention and loyalty in an emerging-market setting, using Uzbekistan as the reference context. Drawing on research on AI in marketing, algorithm aversion, organizational trust and information privacy, the paper positions consumer trust in the AI system as the key mediating mechanism and identifies algorithmic transparency and perceived human oversight as its principal antecedents. Perceived privacy risk and decision involvement are proposed as boundary conditions, and linguistic and cultural fit is introduced as a context-specific component of personalization quality. Five testable propositions are formulated, a four-phase research design is outlined, and managerial implications are presented for firms operating in mobile-first, multilingual markets with fast-growing e-commerce and fintech sectors. The paper concludes with a research agenda for empirical validation.

This study was motivated by the fact that the learning independence of fourth-grade students at SD Negeri 13 Lolong Belanti had not been fully developed despite the implementation of the Merdeka Curriculum. This study aims to describe the learning independence of fourth-grade students under the Merdeka Curriculum and to analyze its impact on students' learning independence. This study employed a qualitative method with a case study approach. Research informants consisted of the school principal, the fourth-grade teacher, and fourth-grade students of SD Negeri 13 Lolong Belanti, selected through purposive sampling. Data were collected through participatory observation, interviews, and documentation, with data validity ensured through source and technique triangulation. Data were analyzed through data reduction, data display, and conclusion drawing. The results show that the implementation of the Merdeka Curriculum had a positive impact on students' learning independence, reflected in five aspects: learning initiative, responsibility, discipline, self-confidence, and intrinsic motivation. Most students demonstrated enthusiasm in seeking information independently, completing tasks on time, complying with classroom rules, expressing opinions confidently, and showing high learning motivation. The Merdeka Curriculum contributes to improving students' learning independence through student-centered learning.

The sub-typing of breast cancer plays a vital role in personalizing oncology by guiding treatment strategies and prognosis. This study proposes a new approach by integrating deep learning and large language models (LLMs) for subtype prediction based on gene expression. The approach includes unsupervised clustering using K-Means so as to identify the hidden expression patterns, followed by a Multi-layer Perceptron Feedforward Neural Network for supervised classification of BRCA subtypes. In order to improve the interpretability, Llama 3.1 model was fine-tuned on prompt response pairs that were derived from gene subtype associations, generating textual explanations for the predicted class. The model gave promising results, with 91 percent accuracy, thus demonstrating strong potential for clinical insight generation. Additionally, the model is tested with dataset of lung cancer, confirming its generalizability among tumour types.
